claim: The temporal lobe is a morphological adaptation of the brain that is unique to primates.
source: The temporal lobe is a morphological adaptation of the brain that is unique to primates (Bryant and Preuss, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bryant and Preuss, 2018.

claim: The origins of the temporal lobe likely include expansion of higher-order visual areas to accompany the primate reliance on vision.
source: Its origins likely include expansion of higher-order visual areas to accompany the primate reliance on vision (Allman, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Allman, 1982.

claim: Temporal association cortex contains areas devoted to higher-level visual processing and social information processing.
source: Temporal association cortex contains areas devoted to higher-level visual processing and social information processing (Rushworth et al., 2013; Sallet et al., 2011) that, in turn, rely strongly on visual information in primates (Perrett et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rushworth et al., 2013 and Sallet et al., 2011.

claim: Higher-level visual processing and social information processing in temporal association cortex rely strongly on visual information in primates.
source: Temporal association cortex contains areas devoted to higher-level visual processing and social information processing (Rushworth et al., 2013; Sallet et al., 2011) that, in turn, rely strongly on visual information in primates (Perrett et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Perrett et al., 1992.

claim: The expanded temporal cortex in apes and humans contains several multimodal areas and areas associated with semantics and language.
source: The expanded temporal cortex in apes and humans contains several multimodal areas and areas associated with semantics and language (Dronkers et al., 2004; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007; Price, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dronkers et al., 2004; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007; and Price, 2000.

claim: Great apes possess an extra sulcus in the temporal cortex, suggesting expansion of this part of cortex.
source: Morphologically, great apes possess an extra sulcus in the temporal cortex, suggesting at the very least expansion of this part of cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations of great ape brains.

claim: A region in the middle part of the superior temporal sulcus of the macaque shares anatomical features of the human temporo-parietal junction area located at the caudal end of the temporal cortex, suggesting a major relocation of this area.
source: Mars et al. (2013) reported a region in the middle part of the superior temporal sulcus of the macaque that shares anatomical features of the human temporo-parietal junction area located at the caudal end of the temporal cortex, suggesting a major relocation of this area.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mars et al., 2013.

claim: Expansion of the temporo-parietal junction and superior temporal sulcus gave rise to a modified ventral visual processing stream to support increased social abilities in humans.
source: In a similar vein, Patel et al. (2019) suggest that expansion of the temporo-parietal junction and superior temporal sulcus gave rise to a modified ventral visual processing stream to support increased social abilities in humans.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Patel et al., 2019.

claim: There is dramatic expansion of the arcuate fasciculus temporal cortex projections in the human.
source: Rilling et al. (2008) first suggested dramatic expansion of the arcuate fasciculus temporal cortex projections in the human, but more recent studies also emphasize increased projections of the middle longitudinal and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi and their role in language-related processes in the human (Catani and Bambini, 2014; Makris et al., 2013; Makris and Pandya, 2009; Saur et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rilling et al., 2008.

claim: There are increased projections of the middle longitudinal and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi in the human and they play a role in language-related processes.
source: Rilling et al. (2008) first suggested dramatic expansion of the arcuate fasciculus temporal cortex projections in the human, but more recent studies also emphasize increased projections of the middle longitudinal and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi and their role in language-related processes in the human (Catani and Bambini, 2014; Makris et al., 2013; Makris and Pandya, 2009; Saur et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Catani and Bambini, 2014; Makris et al., 2013; Makris and Pandya, 2009; and Saur et al., 2008.

claim: Human MT+ complex is located much more ventrally in posterior temporal cortex than its macaque homolog.
source: As a case in point, human MT+ complex is located much more ventrally in posterior temporal cortex than its macaque homolog (Huk et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Huk et al., 2002.

claim: T1w/T2w myelin maps correlate well with cortical myelinization.
source: As primary modality we use surface maps derived from the cortical ribbon of T1- and T2-weighted scans, which have been shown to correlate well with cortical myelinization and which are available for all three species (Glasser et al., 2014; Glasser and Van Essen, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glasser et al., 2014 and Glasser and Van Essen, 2011.

claim: Myelin maps can be used to identify homologous areas across brains and species, such as primary sensory and motor cortex, which is high in myelin, and association cortex, which is low in myelin.
source: Such 'myelin maps' can be used to identify homologous areas across brains and species, such as primary sensory and motor cortex, which is high in myelin, and association cortex, which is low in myelin (Glasser et al., 2014; Large et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glasser et al., 2014 and Large et al., 2016.

claim: The cross-species registration aligns the myelin maps well, with the predicted human maps showing most of the distinctive features of the actual human myelin map.
source: The cross-species registration aligns the myelin maps well, with the predicted human maps showing most of the distinctive features of the actual human myelin map (Figure 2, top row).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual inspection of Figure 2.

claim: Posterior areas such as V1 are well aligned, with the highest myelin evident on the medial part of the occipital cortex, having relocated quite substantially from a more lateral orientation in the macaque.
source: Posterior areas such as V1 are well aligned, with the highest myelin evident on the medial part of the occipital cortex, having relocated quite substantially from a more lateral orientation in the macaque.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the myelin registration results.

claim: The prominent myelin hot spot in the location of the MT+ complex is noticeable in the aligned myelin maps.
source: The prominent myelin hot spot in the location of the MT+ complex is also noticeable.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the myelin registration results.

claim: Areas where the myelin maps showed fewer distinctive features to guide the registration, such as in the prefrontal cortex, showed some differentiation between the predicted and actual human maps.
source: Areas where the myelin maps showed fewer distinctive features to guide the registration, such as in the prefrontal cortex, showed some differentiation between the predicted and actual human maps.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the myelin registration results.

claim: The human and macaque tract maps resemble those obtained in previous studies.
source: The human and macaque tract maps resemble those obtained in previous studies (Mars et al., 2018c; Schmahmann and Pandya, 2009) and the chimpanzee SLF3 and AF are similar to previous reports (Hecht et al., 2015; Rilling et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mars et al., 2018c; Schmahmann and Pandya, 2009; Hecht et al., 2015; and Rilling et al., 2008.

claim: The chimpanzee SLF3 and AF are similar to previous reports.
source: The human and macaque tract maps resemble those obtained in previous studies (Mars et al., 2018c; Schmahmann and Pandya, 2009) and the chimpanzee SLF3 and AF are similar to previous reports (Hecht et al., 2015; Rilling et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hecht et al., 2015 and Rilling et al., 2008.

claim: The chimpanzee MDLF, ILF, and IFO tracts are reported for the first time in this study, apart from a previous exploratory study.
source: The other chimpanzee tracts are reported here for the first time, apart from a previous exploratory study (Mars et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on the novelty of the data presented and a citation to Mars et al., 2019.

claim: The myelin-based registration can predict the tract maps well in both hemispheres, with the notable exception of AF and to a lesser extent ILF and SLF3.
source: In general, it can be observed that the myelin-based registration can predict the tract maps well in both hemispheres, with the notable exception of AF and to a lesser extent ILF and SLF3 (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations from Figure 4.

claim: AF shows the lowest Dice coefficient and the highest extension ratio, indicating that this tract's differential projections in the human brain are not merely due to relocation of areas.
source: AF in particular shows the lowest Dice coefficient and the highest extension ratio (Figure 5A,B), indicating that this tract's differential projections in the human brain are not merely due to relocation of areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The maps for macaque and chimpanzee are overall predicted to a similar degree, with the exception of AF.
source: The maps for macaque and chimpanzee are overall predicted to a similar degree, as can be seen in the overlay and correlation maps, with the exception of AF (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations from Figure 4.

claim: In the left hemisphere, there was no significant main effect of species on extension ratios.
source: In the left hemisphere, there was no significant main effect of species (F(1, 179)=1.38, p=0.47), but a highly significant main effect of tract (F(4, 792)=565.00, p<0.001) and a highly significant interaction effect of species and tract (F(4, 792)=207.73, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: In the left hemisphere, there was a highly significant main effect of tract on extension ratios.
source: In the left hemisphere, there was no significant main effect of species (F(1, 179)=1.38, p=0.47), but a highly significant main effect of tract (F(4, 792)=565.00, p<0.001) and a highly significant interaction effect of species and tract (F(4, 792)=207.73, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: In the left hemisphere, there was a highly significant interaction effect of species and tract on extension ratios.
source: In the left hemisphere, there was no significant main effect of species (F(1, 179)=1.38, p=0.47), but a highly significant main effect of tract (F(4, 792)=565.00, p<0.001) and a highly significant interaction effect of species and tract (F(4, 792)=207.73, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: In the right hemisphere, there was a significant main effect of species on extension ratios.
source: In the right hemisphere, we found a significant main effect of species (F(1, 179)=16.76, p<0.001) as well as a highly significant effect of tract (F(4, 792)=261.94, p<0.001) and a highly significant interaction effect (F(4, 792)=225.70, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: In the right hemisphere, there was a highly significant effect of tract on extension ratios.
source: In the right hemisphere, we found a significant main effect of species (F(1, 179)=16.76, p<0.001) as well as a highly significant effect of tract (F(4, 792)=261.94, p<0.001) and a highly significant interaction effect (F(4, 792)=225.70, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: In the right hemisphere, there was a highly significant interaction effect of species and tract on extension ratios.
source: In the right hemisphere, we found a significant main effect of species (F(1, 179)=16.76, p<0.001) as well as a highly significant effect of tract (F(4, 792)=261.94, p<0.001) and a highly significant interaction effect (F(4, 792)=225.70, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: The actual human tract terminations of MDLF span the superior temporal gyrus and reach the inferior parietal cortex.
source: The actual human tract terminations of MDLF span the superior temporal gyrus and reach the inferior parietal cortex (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations from Figure 4A.

claim: In the macaque and chimpanzee, the actual MDLF terminates in superior temporal gyrus but reaches only to a small part of the inferior parietal cortex.
source: In the macaque and chimpanzee, the actual MDLF terminates in superior temporal gyrus but reaches only to a small part of the inferior parietal cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the tract maps.

claim: When applying the myelin-based registration, macaque and chimpanzee MDLF are both predicted to reach a comparable portion of the human temporal lobe and parts of both angular and supramarginal gyri of the inferior parietal lobe.
source: When applying the myelin-based registration, macaque and chimpanzee MDLF are both predicted to reach a comparable portion of the human temporal lobe and parts of both angular and supramarginal gyri of the inferior parietal lobe (Makris et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of applying the myelin-based registration and is supported by a citation to Makris et al., 2013.

claim: The Dice coefficients for the chimpanzee and macaque MDLF are high and the extension ratio is close to one indicating no tract extension in addition to cortical expansion.
source: The Dice coefficients for the chimpanzee and macaque MDLF are high and the extension ratio is close to one indicating no tract extension in addition to cortical expansion (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The myelin-based registration can predict the parietal cortical projections of SLF3 and IFO to a large degree.
source: A similar observation can be made for the posterior terminations of SLF3 and IFO. The myelin-based registration can predict the parietal cortical projections to a large degree.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the tract maps and registration results.

claim: Expansion and relocation of brain areas are largely sufficient to model the posterior cortical terminations of SLF3 and IFO, while extension of the tract's connectivity pattern plays a minor role in explaining the species differences.
source: Taken together, this suggests that expansion and relocation of brain areas are largely sufficient to model the posterior cortical terminations of SLF3 and IFO, while extension of the tract's connectivity pattern plays a minor role in explaining the species differences.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the registration and tract map results.

claim: The expected occipito-temporal connection of ILF can be modelled well by predicted ILF terminations.
source: Predicted ILF terminations show that the expected occipito-temporal connection can be modelled well (Catani and Thiebaut de Schotten, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on the registration results and is supported by a citation to Catani and Thiebaut de Schotten, 2008.

claim: The extension ratio for ILF is elevated indicating that there is some remaining tract extension that has not been modelled by cortical relocation.
source: The extension ratio for ILF is elevated indicating that there is some remaining tract extension that has not been modelled by cortical relocation.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of the extension ratio.

claim: Human ILF has more extended posterior projections than predicted by the myelin registration.
source: This is also reflected in the tract overlay (Figure 4A), which shows that human ILF has more extended posterior projections than predicted by the myelin registration.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations from Figure 4A.

claim: Human AF reaches anteriorly to inferior and dorsal frontal areas.
source: Human AF reaches anteriorly to inferior and dorsal frontal areas.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the tract maps.

claim: The posterior projections of human AF reach into middle and inferior temporal cortex.
source: The posterior projections of human AF reach into middle and inferior temporal cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the tract maps.

claim: The chimpanzee posterior terminations of AF are in inferior parietal lobe and superior temporal cortex.
source: The chimpanzee posterior terminations are in inferior parietal lobe and superior temporal cortex and in the macaque, the temporal projections reach superior temporal areas.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the tract maps.

claim: In the macaque, the temporal projections of AF reach superior temporal areas.
source: The chimpanzee posterior terminations are in inferior parietal lobe and superior temporal cortex and in the macaque, the temporal projections reach superior temporal areas.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the tract maps.

claim: For AF, the myelin-based registration does not provide a good prediction of the tract map across species, especially for the macaque.
source: For AF, the myelin-based registration does not provide a good prediction of the tract map across species, especially for the macaque.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the registration results.

claim: The correlation map for the chimpanzee AF shows low correlation along the temporal lobe.
source: The correlation map for the chimpanzee shows low correlation along the temporal lobe and for the macaque, correlation values in temporal lobe are extremely low.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the correlation maps.

claim: For the macaque AF, correlation values in temporal lobe are extremely low.
source: The correlation map for the chimpanzee shows low correlation along the temporal lobe and for the macaque, correlation values in temporal lobe are extremely low.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the correlation maps.

claim: AF has the lowest Dice coefficient and the extension ratio is high, especially in the macaque.
source: AF has the lowest Dice coefficient and the extension ratio is high, especially in the macaque, which is in line with overlay and correlation maps.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of Dice coefficients and extension ratios.

claim: The 'failure' of the myelin registration in the temporal lobe indicates that extension and relocation of cortical areas is not sufficient to explain the posterior tract projections of AF, but that the tract extended into new cortical territory in the temporal lobe.
source: The 'failure' of the myelin registration in the temporal lobe indicates that extension and relocation of cortical areas is not sufficient to explain the posterior tract projections of AF, but that the tract extended into new cortical territory in the temporal lobe.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the registration results.

claim: In the inferior parietal lobe, the connectivity fingerprint of actual human and predicted chimpanzee and macaque tract maps are highly similar, except for a small increase in the intensity of ILF indicating tract extension.
source: Figure 5C demonstrates that in the inferior parietal lobe, the connectivity fingerprint of actual human and predicted chimpanzee and macaque tract maps are highly similar, except for a small increase in the intensity of ILF indicating tract extension as discussed above.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations from Figure 5C.

claim: The myelin-derived registration can predict the connectivity profile of the inferior parietal lobe well, despite the local expansion of the cortical sheet.
source: This indicates that the myelin-derived registration can predict this area's connectivity profile well, despite the local expansion of the cortical sheet.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the connectivity fingerprint analysis.

claim: For the temporal vertex, there is a strong mismatch regarding the connectivity profile, in particular regarding the intensities for AF.
source: For the temporal vertex, however, there is a strong mismatch regarding the connectivity profile, in particular regarding the intensities for AF.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the connectivity fingerprint analysis.

claim: The connectional fingerprint of the temporal area is different in the human than would be predicted purely based on cortical relocation.
source: This indicates that the connectional fingerprint of this temporal area is different in the human than would be predicted purely based on cortical relocation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the connectivity fingerprint analysis.

claim: Cortical expansion and resulting relocation of brain areas alone provide a good prediction of several tracts' terminations in posterior temporal and parietal cortex.
source: We showed that cortical expansion and resulting relocation of brain areas alone provide a good prediction of several tracts' terminations in posterior temporal and parietal cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on the overall results of the study.

claim: In the case of AF, an additional change in brain architecture was extension of the tract into new cortical areas independent of cortical expansion and resulting relocation.
source: In the case of AF in particular, we showed that an additional change in brain architecture was extension of the tract into new cortical areas independent of cortical expansion and resulting relocation.
evidence: The claim is based on the overall results of the study.

claim: Previous work has suggested expansion and relocation of areas in posterior temporal cortex and adjacent parietal cortex.
source: Previous work has suggested expansion and relocation of areas in posterior temporal cortex and adjacent parietal cortex (Mars et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2019), which is consistent with the ventral location of MT+ complex in humans compared to other primates.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mars et al., 2013 and Patel et al., 2019.

claim: Similar reorganizations of visual-temporal pathways in the human have been suggested by Haak et al. (2018).
source: Similar reorganizations have been suggested by Haak et al. (2018), who proposed modifications of visual-temporal pathways in the human.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Haak et al., 2018.

claim: The major relocations captured by the myelin registration were demonstrated to predict certain features of white matter tracts, such as the posterior projections of MDLF.
source: These major relocations were captured by our myelin registration and demonstrated to predict certain features of white matter tracts, such as the posterior projections of MDLF.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the study.

claim: Changes in connectivity between humans and other species have been described for a variety of association tracts, including the temporal projections of AF into middle temporal gyrus.
source: Separate from cortical relocation, changes in connectivity between humans and other species have been described for a variety of association tracts, including the temporal projections of AF into middle temporal gyrus (Eichert et al., 2019; Rilling et al., 2008), the frontal projections of SLF3 (Hecht et al., 2015), and expansion of the ventral route consisting of MDLF and IFO (Forkel et al., 2014; Makris et al., 2013; Makris et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eichert et al., 2019 and Rilling et al., 2008.

claim: Changes in connectivity between humans and other species have been described for the frontal projections of SLF3.
source: Separate from cortical relocation, changes in connectivity between humans and other species have been described for a variety of association tracts, including the temporal projections of AF into middle temporal gyrus (Eichert et al., 2019; Rilling et al., 2008), the frontal projections of SLF3 (Hecht et al., 2015), and expansion of the ventral route consisting of MDLF and IFO (Forkel et al., 2014; Makris et al., 2013; Makris et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hecht et al., 2015.

claim: Changes in connectivity between humans and other species have been described for expansion of the ventral route consisting of MDLF and IFO.
source: Separate from cortical relocation, changes in connectivity between humans and other species have been described for a variety of association tracts, including the temporal projections of AF into middle temporal gyrus (Eichert et al., 2019; Rilling et al., 2008), the frontal projections of SLF3 (Hecht et al., 2015), and expansion of the ventral route consisting of MDLF and IFO (Forkel et al., 2014; Makris et al., 2013; Makris et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Forkel et al., 2014; Makris et al., 2013; and Makris et al., 2009.

claim: MDLF and IFO have been suggested to play a role in language functions in the human brain.
source: Both of these latter tracts have been suggested to play a role in language functions in the human brain (Catani and Bambini, 2014; Hagoort, 2016; Makris et al., 2009; Makris and Pandya, 2009; Saur et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Catani and Bambini, 2014; Hagoort, 2016; Makris et al., 2009; Makris and Pandya, 2009; and Saur et al., 2008.

claim: The human tract projections of MDLF can be predicted well by the cortical relocation model.
source: In the case of MDLF, the human tract projections can be predicted well by the cortical relocation model.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the study.

claim: The pattern of cortical terminations of MDLF changed according to the general expansion and relocation of brain areas, without additional extension into new regions of the brain.
source: This indicates that the pattern of cortical terminations changed according to the general expansion and relocation of brain areas, without additional extension into new regions of the brain.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the results of the study.

claim: For ILF, IFO and SLF3, the posterior tract projections can be modelled well, despite the large distortions of target areas within the cortical sheet.
source: For other tracts reaching to temporo-parietal areas, such as ILF, IFO and SLF3, the posterior tract projections can also be modelled well, despite the large distortions of target areas within the cortical sheet.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the study.

claim: ILF, IFO and SLF3 seem to follow the evolutionary scenario where a tract's extension in the human brain can be explained by relocation of areas along the cortical sheet.
source: These tracts seem to follow the evolutionary scenario described in the upper row in Figure 1B,D, where a tract's extension in the human brain can be explained by relocation of areas along the cortical sheet.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the results and reference to Figure 1B,D.

claim: AF showed the lowest consistency across species when applying the myelin-based registration.
source: AF showed the lowest consistency across species when applying the myelin-based registration.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the study.

claim: Dice ratio and extension ratio for AF reflect the increased tract termination especially into the temporal lobes.
source: Dice ratio and extension ratio reflect the increased tract termination especially into the temporal lobes, which can be observed in the tract maps.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis and observations from the tract maps.

claim: AF underwent further evolutionary adaptations that specifically affected the connectivity pattern of AF independent of cortical relocation.
source: This points to further evolutionary adaptations that specifically affected the connectivity pattern of AF independent of cortical relocation, the scenario described in the bottom figure in Figure 1B,D.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the results and reference to Figure 1B,D.

claim: The result for AF is consistent with previous accounts in the literature.
source: Our result is consistent with previous accounts in the literature (Ardesch et al., 2019; Eichert et al., 2019; Rilling et al., 2008), but the approach described here enabled us to formally test this hypothesis in the wider context of cortical reorganization across three primate species and to quantify the species differences.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ardesch et al., 2019; Eichert et al., 2019; and Rilling et al., 2008.

claim: Extension of a tract into new cortical territories alters the unique connectivity fingerprint of the innervated areas, which profoundly changes the computational capabilities that area supports.
source: Importantly, extension of a tract into new cortical territories alters the unique connectivity fingerprint of the innervated areas, which profoundly changes the computational capabilities that area supports (Mars et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mars et al., 2018b.

claim: There are minor extensions of ILF into temporo-parietal cortex.
source: Apart from modifications of AF, we also noted some minor extensions of ILF into temporo-parietal cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the results of the study.

claim: ILF's extension in the human brain is consistent with reports that showed a split of this tract into multiple subtracts due to the expansion of parts of the temporal cortex, including the fusiform gyrus.
source: ILF's extension in the human brain is consistent with reports that that showed a split of this tract into multiple subtracts due to the expansion of parts of the temporal cortex, including the fusiform gyrus (Latini et al., 2017; Roumazeilles et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Latini et al., 2017 and Roumazeilles et al., 2019.

claim: ILF extensions could be related to the increase of cortical territory related to processing social information, such as social networks and faces.
source: This extensions could be related to the increase of cortical territory related to processing social information, such as social networks and faces (Noonan et al., 2018; Sallet et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Noonan et al., 2018 and Sallet et al., 2011.

claim: Parietal SLF3 projections are most prominent in the human brain, which has been linked to our unique capacity of social learning.
source: Previously, it has been shown that parietal SLF3 projections are most prominent in the human brain, which has been linked to our unique capacity of social learning (Hecht et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hecht et al., 2013.

claim: Species differences in the posterior projections of SLF3 can be mostly explained by local expansion of the posterior temporal and parietal cortex.
source: We show that species differences in the posterior projections of SLF3 can be mostly explained by local expansion of the posterior temporal and parietal cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the study.

claim: Cortical expansion can model the terminations of MDLF, a tract which has been linked to visuospatial and integrative audiovisual function.
source: Similarly, we show that cortical expansion can model the terminations of MDLF, a tract, which has been linked to visuospatial and integrative audiovisual function (Makris et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the study and is supported by a citation to Makris et al., 2013.

claim: SLF3 and MDLF didn't undergo additional evolutionary modifications that affected their posterior terminations.
source: Our results thus suggest that SLF3 and MDLF didn't undergo additional evolutionary modifications that affected their posterior terminations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the results of the study.

claim: MSM has become a vital tool for human surface registration.
source: It has become a vital tool for human surface registration (Abdollahi et al., 2014; Garcia et al., 2018; Glasser et al., 2016) and here we demonstrated its utility for cross-species research.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abdollahi et al., 2014; Garcia et al., 2018; and Glasser et al., 2016.

claim: A registration based on T1w/T2w MRI data can match critical landmarks across species.
source: With the presented surface matching method, we showed that a registration based on T1w/T2w MRI data can match critical landmarks across species.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the study.

claim: T1w/T2w maps are sensitive to other features than myelin.
source: T1w/T2w maps are sensitive to other features than myelin and other sequences are sensitive to aspects of cortical myelin (Lutti et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lutti et al., 2014.

claim: Other sequences are sensitive to aspects of cortical myelin.
source: T1w/T2w maps are sensitive to other features than myelin and other sequences are sensitive to aspects of cortical myelin (Lutti et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lutti et al., 2014.

claim: The T1w/T2w maps employed here are similar across species, allowing comparison of like with like.
source: The crucial point is that the maps we employed here are similar across species, allowing us to compare like with like (Glasser et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Glasser et al., 2014.

claim: Projecting data of different modalities to a surface representation is a useful tool for comparative neuroscience.
source: Projecting data of different modalities to a surface representation is a useful tool for comparative neuroscience.
evidence: The claim is based on the methodological approach of the study.

claim: A similar approach has been taken to investigate the relationship between gene expression and myelin content of the cortex.
source: A similar approach has been taken to investigate the relationship between gene expression and myelin content of the cortex (Burt et al., 2018) and gradients of change across multiple modalities of brain organization (Blazquez Freches et al., 2020; Huntenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Burt et al., 2018.

claim: A similar approach has been taken to investigate gradients of change across multiple modalities of brain organization.
source: A similar approach has been taken to investigate the relationship between gene expression and myelin content of the cortex (Burt et al., 2018) and gradients of change across multiple modalities of brain organization (Blazquez Freches et al., 2020; Huntenburg et al., 2018).
